Article Title: Fortnite x Spider-Man Brand New Day revealed: Release date, skins, web shooters, and more
Article Text:
Fortnite x Spider-Man Brand New Day collaboration revealed (Image via Fortnite)

Fortnite x Spider-Man Brand New Day skins

Spider-Man Sprite in Fortnite

The moment Fortnite fans have been waiting for has officially arrived, and Epic Games has finally revealed the upcoming Fortnite Spider-Man Brand New Day collaboration skins. The trailer was officially shared on Sony and Fortnite channels, and it provided an exclusive look at Spider-Man: Brand New Day.Other major highlights of the trailer were the Punisher skin and the Web Shooters. It will be exciting to see all the new content arriving to the game very soon. In the section below, we take a look at everything revealed about Fortnite x Spider-Man Brand New Day.The new trailer posted by Fortnite has struck the fans with excitement and it commenced by providing a brief look at the new Spider-Man skin. The same is essentially based on Tom Holland's appearance in Spider-Man: Brand New Day.The trailer further featured a message from Tom Holland, and he talked about the addition of new outfits based on the upcoming movie. He also mentioned about the return of the Web Shooters, which has been one of the most awaited things.There were two major skin reveals as part of the Fortnite x Spider-Man Brand New Day trailer. The first being the Spider-Man skin based on the appearance of Tom Holland in the new movie.Aside from that, the iconic antihero Punisher has been confirmed to make his Fortnite debut.One of the finest aspects of the new trailer was the reveal of the Punisher skin that will be arriving to the battle royale experience.Essentially, the skin is going to be based on Jon Bernthal's look in the movie. The trailer further provided us with a glance at Punisher and Spider-Man fighting The Hulk in the streets of Battlewoods. Nevertheless, there has been no information about a Hulk skin releasing.The return of the Mythic Web Shooters is arguably the most exciting gameplay development in the entire reveal. After the exclusive look at Spider-Man: Brand New Day, the trailer provided the first glance at the Web Shooters back in action.Adding to the excitement, Epic has revealed that the upcoming Web Shooters Power Hours on August 1, 2026, will feature unlimited Web Shooters for players to use.The leaked Fortnite Spider-Man Sprite was not revealed during the trailer. As a result, there is a chance that the developers could be waiting to reveal it later on. Nevertheless, the same is not confirmed, and you will have to wait for further announcements.Fortnite x Spider-Man Brand New Day skins and related content will be introduced to the battle royale experience after the release of v41.30. The same is set to arrive on July 30, 2026, at 4 AM ET, which falls in line with the release of Spider-Man Brand New Day.The Fortnite x Spider-Man Brand New Day collaboration is shaping up to be one of the biggest crossover events of Chapter 7 Season 3.
Article Summary: The fortnite x spider-man brand new day trailer has been released. The trailer was officially shared on sony and fortnites channels. It provided an exclusive look at the upcoming movie. Other major highlights of the trailer were the punisher skin and the web shooters.

Article Title: One small step for Hyderabad, one giant leap for Vikram-1
Article Text:
India's first private orbital rocket, Vikram-1, blasts off from Sriharikota carrying four satellite payloads

More than a launch, a signal

Why Hyderabad?

Hyderabad's space ecosystem

Skyroot's rise mirrors Hyderabad's ambitions

Dhruva Space gives the ecosystem another pillar

Policy, capital and research converge

Building beyond rockets

Reforms that changed the landscape

From reforms to orbit

Can Hyderabad overtake Bengaluru?

Race for India's space capital

The challenges ahead

Strengths and challenges

A launch that changed the conversation





HYDERABAD: Skyroot's landmark launch has given India's private space ambitions their biggest boost yet. But can one successful mission transform Hyderabad into the country's spacetech capital, or is the harder journey only just beginning?When Skyroot Aerospace's Vikram-1 pierced the skies above Sriharikota on July 18, it did far more than place four satellite payloads into a 450-km low-Earth orbit.For the first time, a privately developed Indian orbital rocket successfully reached orbit, placing India among a small group of countries, including the United States and China, where private companies have independently designed, built and launched orbital rockets.For Hyderabad, however, the significance stretched well beyond a historic countdown.The city's largest spacetech startup had delivered India's most consequential private space milestone, prompting a larger question: is Vikram-1 merely a breakthrough for one company, or has it accelerated Hyderabad's emergence as the country's private space capital?The answer lies not just in a rocket that flew successfully, but in the ecosystem that made it possible.The symbolism surrounding Mission Aagaman was impossible to miss. Vikram-1 lifted off exactly 46 years after ISRO's SLV-3 placed the Rohini satellite into orbit, marking India's arrival as a spacefaring nation in 1980. This time, history repeated itself under very different circumstances.Instead of a government laboratory, the mission was led by a startup founded only eight years ago by former ISRO scientists Pawan Kumar Chandana and Naga Bharath Daka.Built around an all-carbon composite airframe, equipped with in-house propulsion systems and 3D-printed engines, Vikram-1 demonstrated that Indian private industry had matured from building components to developing complete launch vehicles.Its success also reflected the changing structure of India's space programme. Until a few years ago, orbital launches remained the exclusive domain of ISRO. Today, private companies are beginning to share that responsibility, targeting the rapidly expanding market for small satellite launches.As Skyroot CEO Chandana put it after the mission, the launch proved that India possesses "the talent, the technology and the industrial strength to build launch vehicles that meet the world's standards and serve the world from here."The achievement was not merely technical. It validated years of policy reforms aimed at opening India's space sector to private participation, while giving investors, customers and policymakers confidence that Indian startups can compete in one of the world's most technologically demanding industries.It is tempting to view Skyroot's success as the achievement of one ambitious startup. But Vikram-1 is also a story about geography.Unlike India's traditional space establishment, centred largely around Bengaluru and ISRO's network of research centres, much of the country's emerging private launch ecosystem has taken shape in Hyderabad.The city's credentials extend well beyond one company. It hosts Skyroot Aerospace, satellite manufacturer Dhruva Space, Pixxel's growing presence, specialised component manufacturers, defence and aerospace suppliers, research institutions and one of India's most active startup ecosystems.According to the IIIT Hyderabad Centre for Innovation and Entrepreneurship's SpaceTech Ecosystem Report, Hyderabad has steadily evolved into one of India's leading spacetech clusters, driven by a combination of research institutions, manufacturing capability, venture capital, startup incubation and government support.Rather than relying on a single anchor institution, the city has developed an interconnected network linking startups, academia, investors and industry.The report identifies Hyderabad as one of the country's fastest-growing hubs for downstream and upstream space technologies, with strengths ranging from launch vehicles and satellites to propulsion systems, electronics, data analytics and earth observation applications.This ecosystem is significantly different from the government-driven model that defined India's space sector for decades.Founded in 2018, Skyroot Aerospace emerged at a time when India's private space ecosystem was still finding its footing.Its founders had spent years at ISRO before deciding that India's future space ambitions required private launch capability alongside government missions.Their first milestone came in 2022 with Vikram-S, India's first privately built sub-orbital rocket. Vikram-1 represents a far bigger leap: from reaching space briefly to successfully entering orbit.That journey has been accompanied by rapid institutional growth. The company has attracted more than $160 million in funding from investors including GIC, Temasek, BlackRock and Sherpalo Ventures, while becoming India's first spacetech unicorn.Its newly established Infinity manufacturing facility near Hyderabad airport is expected to eventually support a production cadence of one rocket every month.According to Skyroot Aerospace, the company is also developing the heavier-lift Vikram-II launch vehicle, capable of carrying up to 900 kg to low-Earth orbit (600 kg to Sun-Synchronous Orbit), alongside reusable launch technologies designed to reduce launch costs while scaling manufacturing at its Infinity campus.Together, these reflect its ambition to move from demonstration missions to regular commercial launches.Equally important is what Skyroot has created beyond its own factory floor. The company's maiden orbital mission involved more than 1,000 employees and nearly 400 suppliers across India, illustrating how private launch vehicles require extensive domestic supply chains spanning precision manufacturing, electronics, materials, software and testing.For Hyderabad, that supplier network could prove as important as the rocket itself.If Skyroot represents Hyderabad's launch ambitions, Dhruva Space reflects the city's growing strength in satellite manufacturing.According to Dhruva Space, the Hyderabad-headquartered company has evolved into an end-to-end space engineering firm, offering satellite platforms, payload integration, launch support, mission operations and ground-station infrastructure, illustrating how the city's spacetech ecosystem now extends well beyond launch vehicles.Unlike launch companies that operate mission by mission, satellite manufacturers participate across the broader lifecycle of space programmes, from design and integration to operations.Dhruva's growing manufacturing capabilities, multiple customer missions and continued expansion suggest Hyderabad's spacetech ambitions are not dependent on a single success story.That distinction matters. Globally successful space clusters rarely emerge around one flagship company alone. Silicon Valley is not defined only by Apple, nor Seattle only by Boeing.Sustainable ecosystems are built when specialised companies operate across complementary segments of the value chain. Hyderabad increasingly appears to be moving in that direction.Industry observers often argue that successful innovation clusters require three ingredients: talent, capital and policy support. Hyderabad appears to be assembling all three.The Telangana government's SpaceTech Framework positions the sector as a strategic growth area, focusing on infrastructure creation, startup support, industry partnerships, research collaboration and skill development.The framework aims to build an ecosystem capable of supporting companies across manufacturing, launch services, satellite technologies and downstream applications.Chief Minister A Revanth Reddy has repeatedly described aerospace as one of Telangana's priority sectors, arguing that companies like Skyroot demonstrate the state's growing capabilities in advanced manufacturing and deep technology.The government has also linked aerospace expansion with broader ambitions of positioning Telangana as a global innovation hub by 2047.Research institutions are playing an equally significant role.The IIIT Hyderabad report notes that universities and research centres have become increasingly important in nurturing spacetech entrepreneurship by producing skilled engineers, supporting applied research and connecting startups with investors and industry partners.Instead of operating in isolation, startups benefit from access to a wider innovation ecosystem that encourages experimentation and commercialisation.That ecosystem is further strengthened by Hyderabad's existing strengths in information technology, defence manufacturing, electronics and precision engineering, industries that naturally complement spacetech development.If Skyroot has become the face of Hyderabad's spacetech ambitions, the city is equally betting on the ecosystem that nurtures companies long before they reach the launch pad.Among the most prominent enablers is T-Hub, which has increasingly focused on deep-tech ventures, including spacetech.Through its Orbit SpaceTech programme, launched in collaboration with industry and ecosystem partners, T-Hub aims to help startups working across satellite technologies, downstream applications, manufacturing and space-enabled services move from prototype to commercialisation.While only a handful of startups may eventually build launch vehicles, the broader value chain, from components and electronics to software, analytics and earth observation, offers far greater opportunities for new companies.That approach aligns with Hyderabad's larger strategy of creating an integrated ecosystem rather than relying solely on a few flagship startups.Even the strongest startup ecosystem would have struggled without a policy shift at the national level.The opening of India's space sector in 2020 fundamentally altered the industry's trajectory.The creation of the Indian National Space Promotion and Authorisation Centre (IN-SPACe) provided private companies with a regulatory framework to access ISRO facilities, seek launch authorisations and participate in activities that were previously reserved almost entirely for the national space agency.Skyroot's own founders have acknowledged that ISRO and IN-SPACe played an important role in supporting Mission Aagaman through technical guidance and timely clearances.Following Vikram-1's successful mission, ISRO Chairman V Narayanan described the launch as "the outcome of years of innovation, perseverance and engineering excellence" and said it reflected "the growing maturity of India's private space sector."He added that ISRO and IN-SPACe remained committed to building a globally competitive ecosystem alongside private industry.IN-SPACe Chairman Pawan Goenka echoed that sentiment, calling the launch "an India moment" and noting that more than 1,000 people and nearly 400 suppliers contributed to the mission.The achievement, he said, demonstrated the industrial capability India had developed over the past few years.The pace of growth has been remarkable. According to government data cited by PIB and IN-SPACe, India has gone from having just one recognised space startup at the beginning of the reforms to more than 400 today.While these companies are spread across the country, Hyderabad has emerged as one of the largest beneficiaries of the liberalised policy environment.Yet calling Hyderabad India's space capital today would be premature.Bengaluru remains the country's undisputed institutional centre for space activity.It houses ISRO headquarters, several major ISRO centres, the headquarters of NewSpace India Limited (NSIL), numerous defence laboratories, public-sector aerospace companies and decades of accumulated engineering expertise.Much of India's satellite development, mission planning and advanced research continues to be anchored there.Karnataka's draft Space Policy also seeks to strengthen Bengaluru's long-standing aerospace ecosystem by encouraging commercial manufacturing, private launch capability and downstream space services, underscoring the growing competition among states to attract spacetech investments.The city also benefits from an established aerospace manufacturing base, a mature venture capital ecosystem and one of the country's deepest pools of engineering talent.Chennai, meanwhile, has begun carving out its own niche through companies such as Agnikul Cosmos, which successfully tested its semi-cryogenic Agnibaan launch vehicle.Tamil Nadu's draft Space Policy further signals the state's intention to attract manufacturing, launch support services and private investment.Against these competitors, Hyderabad's strengths are different. Rather than inheriting a legacy government ecosystem, the city has built momentum around private enterprise.Skyroot, Dhruva Space and several emerging startups represent a younger ecosystem that is being shaped alongside policy reforms rather than decades before them.The IIIT Hyderabad report notes that this concentration of startups, investors, incubators and academic institutions gives the city a distinct advantage in commercial innovation.At the same time, it cautions that sustaining growth will depend on strengthening manufacturing capacity, talent pipelines, financing and collaboration across institutions.For all the optimism generated by Vikram-1, Hyderabad's ambitions still face significant hurdles.The first is scale, a single successful launch, however historic, does not establish a commercially proven launch provider.As Skyroot itself has acknowledged, Vikram-1 remains a technology validation mission.Commercial confidence will depend on repeated successful launches over the coming years.Manufacturing presents another challenge.While Hyderabad has developed strengths in aerospace, defence and electronics, building a globally competitive launch ecosystem requires specialised suppliers capable of producing propulsion systems, avionics, composite materials and precision components at scale.Expanding that industrial base will take sustained investment beyond a few high-profile startups.Funding is another critical factor. Space technology remains among the most capital-intensive industries in the world.Developing rockets, satellites and associated infrastructure demands long investment cycles with uncertain returns.Although Skyroot has attracted significant global funding and achieved unicorn status, maintaining investor confidence across the wider ecosystem will depend on commercial success rather than technological milestones alone.Talent, too, will become increasingly important.As more companies enter the sector, competition for experienced aerospace engineers, propulsion specialists, software developers and systems engineers is likely to intensify.Hyderabad's universities and research institutions will have to expand their role in producing specialised talent if the ecosystem is to sustain long-term growth.Infrastructure will also determine whether momentum translates into leadership.Testing facilities, manufacturing clusters, supply-chain resilience, regulatory support and stronger industry-academia partnerships will all be necessary if Hyderabad hopes to compete with established global space clusters.Perhaps Vikram-1's greatest contribution lies not in the payloads it carried into orbit but in the questions it has forced the industry to ask.Until recently, India's private space story centred largely on aspirations.Companies spoke about building rockets, attracting investment and competing globally. Vikram-1 transformed those ambitions into demonstrated capability.For Hyderabad, that distinction matters.The city is no longer simply home to promising spacetech startups; it is home to India's first private company to place an orbital rocket into space, a growing satellite manufacturer in Dhruva Space, a supportive policy framework, active startup incubators, globally recognised research institutions and an increasingly sophisticated network of suppliers and investors.Whether that combination ultimately earns Hyderabad the title of India's space capital remains uncertain.Bengaluru still possesses unmatched institutional depth, while Chennai is steadily strengthening its own launch ecosystem.Leadership in the space economy will not be determined by a single mission or a single company, but by the ability to continuously innovate, manufacture, attract talent and serve a rapidly expanding global market.Vikram-1 has undoubtedly given Hyderabad unprecedented momentum.But the city's claim to becoming India's space capital will ultimately rest not on one historic launch, but on whether it can build an enduring ecosystem where many more such missions become routine rather than remarkable.
Article Summary: India's first private orbital rocket, vikram-1, blasts off from sriharikota. Skyroot aerospace's landmark launch has given india's private space ambitions their biggest boost yet. But can one successful mission transform hyderabad into the country's spacetech capital, or is the harder journey only just beginning?

Article Title: ICMR hands over homegrown cervical pre-cancer treatment, vaccine technologies to pharma firms
Article Text:
ICMR transfers medical technologies under Patent Mitra Initiative

NEW DELHI: A potential new treatment for cervical pre-cancer and two next-generation vaccines against typhoid and other gut infections have moved a step closer to becoming available in India after the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) licensed the technologies to Indian pharmaceutical companies. If successful, the indigenous products could improve access to affordable treatment and vaccines while reducing dependence on imported technologies.The technologies have been transferred under ICMR’s Medical Innovations Patent Mitra initiative, which helps convert government-funded research into products that can be developed, tested and eventually brought to the market.Among them is SHetA2, a potential treatment for Cervical Intraepithelial Neoplasia (CIN), a precancerous condition caused by persistent infection with the human papillomavirus (HPV). If left untreated, CIN can progress to cervical cancer, one of the leading cancers among Indian women.Unlike surgery, which is commonly used to remove abnormal cells, SHetA2 is designed to selectively destroy HPV-infected abnormal cells while sparing healthy cells. Scientists believe it could offer women a safer and less invasive treatment option in the future. The technology has been licensed to Emcure Pharmaceuticals for further development, clinical testing and commercialisation.ICMR has also licensed two vaccine technologies developed by its National Institute for Research in Bacterial Infections (NIRBI), Kolkata, to Biological E. One is a next-generation vaccine against typhoid, while the other is designed to protect against typhoid, paratyphoid and Shigella, bacteria that cause severe diarrhoea and other intestinal infections, particularly among children.The vaccine candidates will now undergo further development and evaluation before they can be considered for regulatory approval and public use.Dr Rajiv Bahl, Secretary, Department of Health Research, and Director General, ICMR, said partnerships between researchers and industry are helping move promising discoveries from laboratories to patients while strengthening India’s biomedical innovation ecosystem.The technology transfer is part of ICMR’s broader effort to support indigenous healthcare innovation through patent protection, technology licensing, clinical validation and regulatory facilitation, with the aim of making affordable medicines and vaccines available to patients.
Article Summary: Icmr transfers medical technologies under patent mitra initiative. Potential new treatment for cervical pre-cancer and two next-generation vaccines against typhoid and other gut infections. If successful, the indigenous products could improve access to affordable treatment and vaccines while reducing dependence on imported technologies.

Article Title: Trump bans new Chinese robots and power inverters over security fears
Article Text:
The measures will prohibit the import of new humanoid and quadruped robots from China.

NEW DELHI: The Trump administration has introduced sweeping restrictions on imports of new Chinese-made robots and power inverters, saying the move is aimed at protecting the United States' artificial intelligence supply chain and critical infrastructure from potential security risks.The measures, announced by the Federal Communications Commission on Tuesday, prohibit the import of new humanoid and quadruped robots from China, along with connected power inverters used to link renewable energy systems and battery storage to electricity grids and data centre equipment.The restrictions take effect immediately but apply only to models that have not yet been released. However, the FCC retains the authority to withdraw approval for products that are already authorised for sale in the United States.Explaining the decision, the FCC said the targeted products could expose the country to supply chain risks and cyber threats."These devices could create supply chain vulnerabilities that could disrupt US economic and national security and could create a cybersecurity risk that threatened American critical infrastructure," the agency said.FCC Chairman Brendan Carr added, "The FCC will continue to do our part to secure America’s critical supply chains."The latest action reflects the Trump administration's broader effort to reduce reliance on Chinese technology in sectors considered vital to the United States' AI ambitions. Officials believe shifting manufacturing to the US will strengthen domestic industries expected to see rapid growth while reducing the risk of disruption, cyberattacks and theft of sensitive data.The Chinese Embassy in Washington criticised the move and urged the United States to reconsider its approach.It said Beijing "urges the United States to heed the objective and rational voices of the business communities in both countries" and "stop smearing Chinese companies and threatening them with sanctions."The embassy also warned that China would "take all necessary measures in response to any action that causes material harm to its interests."The restrictions come as demand for AI-powered humanoid robots and data centres is expected to rise sharply over the coming years. Industry analysts believe these technologies will play an increasingly important role in manufacturing, logistics and consumer applications, while data centres will require dependable power infrastructure to support expanding AI capabilities.US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has previously warned that Chinese AI companies could face sanctions if they are found to have stolen American intellectual property.Washington is also seeking to avoid becoming heavily dependent on China for another critical technology after Beijing used its dominance in rare earth minerals, which are essential for advanced manufacturing, as leverage in international negotiations.According to sources familiar with the matter, the FCC is expected to exempt many non-Chinese suppliers from the new restrictions, similar to exemptions granted under previous measures targeting foreign drones and networking equipment.Among the companies likely to be affected is Unitree, one of China's leading humanoid robot manufacturers. Counterpoint Research estimates the company holds nearly one-fifth of the global humanoid robot market. Unitree was recently added to the Pentagon's list of companies allegedly linked to the Chinese military, a designation that often precedes tougher restrictions by Washington.The company recently partnered with Nvidia to use the US firm's Blackwell AI chips in its robots. Nvidia has said data collected by the robots remains in the United States and that Unitree's largest customers are American universities and research institutions.US officials and lawmakers have raised concerns that advanced robots could collect sensitive information, interfere with critical operations or be exploited by foreign intelligence agencies."Robots collect data that could be leveraged by malign actors to surveil Americans, enhance the capabilities of foreign intelligence services, or to remotely commandeer the robots," the FCC said.Representative John Moolenaar, who chairs the House Select Committee on China, welcomed the decision and said it would strengthen the US robotics industry while protecting national security.The restrictions also affect Chinese-made power inverters, a market dominated by companies such as Sungrow Power Supply and Huawei. Both firms have expanded their presence internationally by offering lower-cost products, although Huawei already faces extensive US sanctions.US authorities have been examining the security risks linked to Chinese inverters following similar concerns raised in Europe and fears that such equipment could be used to disrupt power systems or install malicious software.The move also reflects Washington's efforts to prevent cyber campaigns similar to Volt Typhoon, a China-linked hacking operation uncovered in 2023 in which attackers allegedly compromised privately owned routers to conceal attempts to infiltrate critical US infrastructure.The US Department of Defense already prohibits the procurement of solar photovoltaic cells, modules and inverters produced by entities regarded as foreign security concerns, including Chinese companies.
Article Summary: The measures will prohibit the import of new humanoid and quadruped robots from china. The restrictions take effect immediately but apply only to models that have not yet been released. The fcc retains the authority to withdraw approval for products that are already authorised for sale in the united states.

Article Title: Vietnam moves to bar under-16s from posting, commenting on social media
Article Text:
Poll Vote & Share your view Do you support the idea of requiring social media accounts for children under 16 to be registered through a parent or guardian? Yes, it enhances safety No, it restricts freedom 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Vietnam is planning to require social media platforms to stop users under the age of 16 from posting content, commenting or reacting to posts, under a draft decree aimed at strengthening online protections for children, according to a document reviewed by Reuters.The proposed rules would require social media accounts belonging to children under 16 to be registered using the information of a parent or legal guardian, who would be responsible for supervising the content viewed by children and the amount of time they spend on the platforms.The draft decree also requires social media companies to use technical measures to identify child users and ensure that they receive age-appropriate content. Platforms would have to provide the highest level of privacy protection for child accounts and proactively detect, warn and block access to content related to violence, pornography, gambling, drugs, suicide and other harmful material."The primary objective is not to ban or excessively restrict children's access to social media, but rather to ensure that when children use social media services, they are placed in an age-appropriate environment and protected from inappropriate risks," deputy culture minister Phan Tam said on Thursday during a meeting to discuss the proposed rules.The proposal comes as governments across the world tighten regulations on children's use of social media amid growing concerns over online safety and the impact of harmful content on young users' mental health.Earlier this week, French lawmakers approved a ban on social media access for children under 15. Australia became the first country to impose such a ban, while several other countries are considering similar measures.The draft decree also proposes new restrictions on online gaming by minors. Game operators would be required to verify users' ages, register accounts of children under 16 through a parent or legal guardian, and limit users under 16 to a maximum of 60 minutes of gameplay per day across games offered by the same company.The draft decree has not yet been finalised and may be revised before it is formally adopted.
Article Summary: Vietnam is planning to require social media platforms to stop users under the age of 16 from posting content, commenting or reacting to posts. The draft decree is aimed at strengthening online protections for children, according to a document reviewed by reuters. Platforms would have to provide the highest level of privacy protection for child accounts.

Article Title: After hacking into world's biggest repository of AI models Hugging Face, OpenAI's rogue AI agent 'attacked' another tech company
Article Text:
Modal Labs says OpenAI's rogue agent exploited its customer code

Modal Labs says customer code, not its platform, was exploited



OpenAI says rogue AI accessed four accounts

The rogue AI agent that carried out a cyberattack on AI platform Hugging Face also compromised a customer hosted by another technology company, Modal Labs, reports Reuters citing a company executive and sources familiar with the matter. The latest details suggest the OpenAI-tested AI agent reached more systems than previously known during its hacking spree earlier this month. While Modal said its own platform was not breached, the incident has raised fresh questions about the risks of autonomous AI systems after the agent exploited vulnerable code before launching a wider attack on Hugging Face, according to a Reuters report.According to a timeline published by Hugging Face on Tuesday, the rogue AI agent first broke into a sandbox, or an isolated testing environment, hosted on a third-party provider's infrastructure before using it to launch the broader attack.Modal's Chief Technology Officer Akshat Bubna confirmed to Reuters that the third-party provider was Modal. He said the AI agent exploited vulnerable code written by one of Modal's customers that was hosted on the company's platform.According to Modal, the customer had "published an unauthenticated endpoint that allowed anyone on the internet to use their sandboxes for code execution," effectively leaving a system open to attackers."Modal's platform or isolation were not compromised in any way," Bubna said.OpenAI declined to comment specifically on the Modal incident. Instead, it referred the news agency to an update in which it said the rogue AI agent had broken into four accounts across four separate services.While the company did not identify those services, a person familiar with the matter identified Modal as one of them, says Reuters report.OpenAI also said it had not found "any other activity at the level of severity or scale of what we've shared related to Hugging Face, which involved a platform-level compromise."
Article Summary: Openai says rogue ai accessed four accounts across four separate services. Latest details suggest the openai-tested ai agent reached more systems than previously known during its hacking spree earlier this month. Modal labs says customer code, not its platform, was exploited by the rogue ai agent.

Article Title: American billionaire Mark Cuban to CEOs: Stop getting ‘shocked’ by healthcare costs, turn to your HR Head as HR is …
Article Text:
Hidden costs in healthcare contracts



AI as a solution



Read Mark Cuban’s complete post here



CEOs turn to their Head of HR. HR is understaffed. They are being asked to take care of all their employees and families and all the issues associated with keeping them as healthy and sane and productive give as possible.

It’s an impossible job.

When I talk to that Head of HR, they say they have to trust the big insurance carriers who are their ASO and PBM. They have no choice but to

On one hand their members are terrified to change their insurance carriers for fear of losing their doctor, or other continuity issues

The vertically integrated conglomerates that own the ASO, PBM, ClearingHouse and so many more companies that have contracts with the employer , know they are afraid to change , so they take advantage

Even when that employer uses a consultant or broker , there is probably a 50pct or greater chance the broker/consultant doesn’t want to go through the work of changing, they would rather collect their fees and not change.

There are even reporting requirements (Form 5500) to disclose these costs, but the ceo has no clue about them.

All this leads to lack of change. Even when every penny they save goes right to the bottom line and increases their stock price

What I told a ceo today ? Take a off of all of your healthcare contracts and put it in your Claude , ChatGPT, grok, Gemini, whatever and use this prompt

“Where are they ripping me off “

They are always shocked.

American billionaire and entrepreneur Mark Cuban has urged the US CEOs to rethink how they manage employee healthcare, warning that executives are overspending because they lack visibility into complex insurance contracts. In a post shared on social media platform X (formerly known as Twitter) Cuban said leaders often turn to their HR leads, who are “understaffed” and overwhelmed. “They are being asked to take care of all their employees and families and all the issues associated with keeping them as healthy and sane and productive as possible,” he wrote.Cuban also argued that vertically integrated conglomerates which own administrative service organisations (ASOs), pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs), and clearinghouses — exploit employers’ reluctance to switch providers. Brokers and consultants, he added, often discourage changes because of the extra work involved. “The vertically integrated conglomerates… know they are afraid to change, so they take advantage,” Cuban said.Cuban recommended CEOs use AI tools to review healthcare contracts and uncover hidden costs. “What I told a CEO today? Take all of your healthcare contracts and put it in your Claude, ChatGPT, Grok, Gemini, whatever and use this prompt: ‘Where are they ripping me off?’ They are always shocked,” he wrote.
Article Summary: Cuban: ceos are overspending because they lack visibility into complex insurance contracts. He said leaders often turn to their hr leads, who are ‘understaffed’ and overwhelmed. “the vertically integrated conglomerates… know they are afraid to change, so they take advantage,” cuban said.

Google Cloud

Article Title: Microsoft AI chief Mustafa Suleyman sees a warning in Sam Altman's AI model hacking Hugging Face; says: They need to be handled ...
Article Text:
Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman

Race for cyber defense accelerates



Microsoft’s AI chief, Mustafa Suleyman, has dubbed a recent cyber incident involving a ‘runaway’ OpenAI agent as a major “warning shot” for the tech industry, emphasising the growing risks posed by autonomous artificial intelligence (AI). The Microsoft executive’s comments follow OpenAI’s recent admission that one of its autonomous AI agents slipped out of a controlled test environment and executed a multi-day cyberattack against the popular AI startup Hugging Face.Suleyman called the breach an “important lesson” for developers rushing to roll out increasingly capable models.“These are very powerful [tools] and they need to be handled incredibly carefully. And we need extreme attention to detail,” Suleyman said in an interview with the Financial Times, adding, “The precautionary principle is going to matter here as the models get more and more powerful and I think it’s a warning shot.”The Hugging Face breach has heightened concerns across Silicon Valley about AI’s potential to discover and exploit software vulnerabilities autonomously. Industry scrutiny has centred on Anthropic’s powerful Mythos model, released in April, as well as OpenAI's aggressive push to build competitive AI cyber tools.Microsoft executives argue that building stronger AI-driven defensive capabilities is the only way to safeguard systems against increasingly sophisticated threats.“Attackers have [these] models. So we have to evaluate and push so that the defenders can defend. It’s not like we have a choice,” said Hayete Gallot, Microsoft’s security chief.Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang talked about the hacking and converted the incident into an opportunity to bring the top AI labs together as ‘defenders’“Attackers have frontier AI. Defenders need a frontier AI ecosystem—the best open and closed models, force-multiplied by a global community,” Huang said in a post on X (formerly Twitter).“During the Hugging Face incident, closed AI blocked essential forensics. An open-weight frontier model helped contain the intrusion. That’s why we created the Open Secure AI Alliance,” he added.
Article Summary: Mustafa suleyman, microsoft's ai chief, calls recent cyber incident a major ‘warning shot’ for the tech industry. Openai admitted that one of its autonomous ai agents slipped out of a controlled test environment and executed a multi-day cyberattack against the popular ai startup hugging face.

Article Title: Why are investors and analysts so worried about Nvidia in the month that CEO Jesen Huang has signed deals worth $500 billion-plus
Article Text:
Why analysts are nervous



Wall Street’s split view



Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang doesn't believe in work-life balance



With a market valuation of nearly $5 trillion, chipmaker Nvidia sits at the centre of global trade. The company that sells GPUs to hyperscalers like Microsoft and Amazon, who then rent the Nvidia-powered compute to startups like OpenAI and Anthropic. Nvidia has also made direct investments in many of those startups giving it exposure to nearly every layer of the AI ecosystem. Put simply, Nvidia profits from almost every stage of AI infrastructure spending. However, a recent report by Business Insider suggests that both investors and analysts are worried as Nvidia has signed deals worth $500 billion. In just a span of few days, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang announced flurry of partnerships and investments:* $500 billion partnership with SK Group (July 24)* $1 billion investment in Naver to build South Korea’s sovereign AI infrastructure (July 24)* $250 billion financing backstop for OpenAI’s Ohio data center (July 26)* Up to $350 billion financing for OpenAI chip purchases (July 26)* Deepened partnership with Safe Superintelligence, founded by Ilya Sutskever (July 27)As reported by BI, despite these blockbuster deals, investors worry the AI ecosystem is becoming too circular — with Nvidia financing the very companies that buy its chips. This raises questions about whether spending reflects genuine demand or simply reinforces itself. If one part of the trade falters, the interconnected structure could drag down the rest. Right on cue, markets reacted: Nvidia shares fell 5% on Monday, surrendering its crown as the world’s most valuable company to Apple. Meanwhile, credit-default swap prices spiked, showing investors are increasingly skittish about Nvidia’s obligations.Bernstein analyst Stacy Rasgon reaffirmed a buy rating and $315 price target, suggesting 60% upside. At Monday’s close, 78 of 81 analysts tracked by Bloomberg still rated Nvidia a buy. Yet the timing is critical: hyperscalers Microsoft, Meta, and Amazon are set to report earnings this week, with investors closely watching their capex guidance. Heavy spending has rattled markets before — Alphabet’s forecast last week triggered a sell-off.Recently, Nvidia CEO has openly admitted that he's on the clock from the second he opens his eyes to the moment he falls asleep, seven days a week, holidays included. There's no switch-off button in his day, and he doesn't seem to be looking for one. And he has admitted that functions well for him. He said that his work life balance is really great. Speaking to Stripe CEO Patrick Collison in an interview in 2024, Huang emphasised that it isn't just the hours, it's how deeply work has taken over his headspace even during downtime. He further added that when he's technically "off," his mind is still running the business in the background.
Article Summary: Investors and analysts worried as nvidia signs deals worth $500 billion. Investors worry the ai ecosystem is becoming too circular. Nvidia profits from almost every stage of ai infrastructure spending. If one part of the trade falters, the interconnected structure could drag down the rest.

Article Title: As users' private chats with Claude appear on Google, Anthropic says: They are to blame as ...
Article Text:
What Anthropic said on the leaked chats of users

What went wrong

Privacy risks ahead

A trove of seemingly private conversations with Anthropic’s Claude chatbot appeared in Google Search results recently, sparking alarm after users discovered sensitive information including cryptocurrency wallet keys and personal details which have been exposed inadvertently. According to a report by Fortune, the issue was traced to Claude’s ‘share’ feature which enables users to generate a link to send a conversation to others.AI giant Anthropic said that the company itself did not make chats searchable, instead blaming the way users shared links. “We give people control over sharing their Claude conversations publicly, and in keeping with our privacy principles, we do not share chat directories or sitemaps with search engines like Google,” a spokesperson told Fortune. The company emphasised that links are only accessible if users choose to share them, but once shared, they can be archived by third-party services.As per the report by Fortune, members of a Reddit discussion channel has discovered that typing some search phrases in Google pulled up a long lists of shared Claude conversations and Claude Artifacts — itself did not make chats searchable, instead blaming the way users shared links.“We give people control over sharing their Claude conversations publicly, and in keeping with our privacy principles, we do not share chat directories or sitemaps with search engines like Google,” a spokesperson told Fortune. The company emphasized that links are only accessible if users choose to share them, but once shared, they can be archived by third-party services.Anthropic has since fixed the issue, removing the links from Google search, though previously shared URLs remain accessible to anyone who already has them. The incident is not unique: last year, a similar glitch exposed nearly 100,000 ChatGPT conversations, while Elon Musk’s Grok chatbot also suffered from the same vulnerability. The problem stems from how “share” features create unique URLs that can be indexed by search engines.Experts warn that shared chatbot conversations often contain more sensitive information than shared documents, since users treat AI assistants as places to “think out loud” about work, health, or legal issues. As Anthropic, OpenAI, and xAI each struggle with versions of the same mistake, the episode underscores how difficult it has been for the industry to permanently fix privacy risks tied to shared AI chats.

Article Title: Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 review: Opens new chapter in foldables; offering distinct experience, design and ultra productivity
Article Text:
1

2

Rating: 4/5



Design

Display

Performance

Camera

Battery

Verdict

Seven generations in, Samsung did something that most people did not expect from a company that had refined the same basic foldable blueprint since 2019. Rather than simply making the Z Fold 8 thinner, faster, or slightly better in every expected dimension, Samsung introduced an entirely new form factor. The Galaxy Z Fold 8 is wider, shorter, and shaped nothing like the tall narrow books that preceded it. It is the most genuinely different Fold Samsung has ever made, and whether that difference is a good thing depends almost entirely on what you want to do with it. Identical to the shape of a passport, Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 comes with a starting price tag of Rs 1,79,999 and is powered by the flagship Snapdragon Elite 8 Gen 5 chipset. Running Android 17, the foldable smartphone features a 50MP dual camera and a 4,800 mAh battery. We used this lightest Galaxy Z Fold yet from Samsung for sometime and here’s our complete review of the same.Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 looks nothing like the last year launched Galaxy Z Fold 7. The compact Galaxy Z Fold 8 is Samsung’s first wide-screen foldable smartphone which is light in weight and is identical to the shape of a passport.The smartphone features a super wide front and main displays. Holding the smartphone folded for the first time produces a unique moment of surprise and makes you think that this does not look or feel like a Fold. This latest foldable smartphone from Samsung comes across like a well-built notebook that happens to open into a tablet. Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 comes with an armor aluminum frame and Gorilla Glass Victus protection offers a premium, yet durable feel throughout. Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 undoubtedly offers a solid build quality which easily communicates the flagship intent in every detail. The company has also redesigned the hinge to both reduce the visibility of the crease by 20% and also to achieve a slimmer profile when folded. The action of folding and unfolding the device is also smooth and precise in a way that reflects seven generations of hinge refinement.Weighing just 201 grams, the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 is lighter as compared to the previous generation Fold and its wider and shorter footprint makes it noticeably easier to carry than the tall narrow form factor of other foldable smartphones available in the market. Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 sits more naturally in a shirt and jeans pocket and it also takes up less space in a bag. Also, the folded device has a compactness that makes it feel considerably less conspicuous in daily life than earlier Fold generations.The button placement is also done well keeping in mind the user experience. The power button and volume rockers are placed on the right side and are easily accessible. The SIM card tray sits on the top and the USB Type C charging port is located at the bottom. The rear of the smartphone houses the dual camera placed vertically in the top left corner. The foldable smartphone comes with IP48 rating which makes it resistant to dust and water. Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 comes in three colour options and the overall aesthetic is clean and considered — a device that looks like it belongs in the premium tier rather than one that is trying to announce itself. For a phone whose form factor is already a conversation starter, the restrained design language is the right call.The front display on the Galaxy Z Fold 8 measures 5.5-inch, which seems small, but its wide 10:16 aspect ratio makes it easy on the eyes, whether you're scrolling through short-form content or typing with two hands. That aspect ratio is the key shift from every previous Fold. Instead of the narrow, slightly awkward candy-bar cover that made quick tasks on previous models feel like using a phone designed for someone with unusually narrow thumbs, the Z Fold 8's cover display feels like a proper phone screen.In practice, this changes the daily rhythm of using the device more than any specification improvement could. Replying to messages, checking notifications, scrolling through a news feed, taking a quick photo — all of these feel natural on the folded cover display in a way that previous Fold covers did not quite manage. The wide proportions mean two-thumb typing works without the cramped feeling that narrow cover displays impose, which removes one of the most consistent irritations of the Fold ownership experience.The main 7.6-inch display has a 4:3 aspect ratio that is better suited for watching video than the square panel on the Ultra. Flip the Fold 8 around and you get a 3:4 aspect ratio that is great for browsing the web or reading ebooks. That orientation flexibility is the inner display's most distinctive quality, and it is what makes the wider form factor argument most convincing in extended use.Content consumption on the inner display is genuinely better than on previous Fold generations. Films play with less of the awkward letterboxing that taller, narrower inner displays produce. Split-screen multitasking feels balanced rather than squeezed. Web browsing in portrait orientation reads like a tablet, and rotating to landscape produces something closer to a widescreen laptop than any phone display has previously managed.The inner display is one of the brightest and smoothest foldable OLED panels available, and the redesigned hinge has reduced crease visibility to the point where it takes deliberate effort to notice it rather than being the first thing your eye goes to. In bright lighting conditions the crease is still visible on close inspection, but it has crossed a threshold where it stops being a daily irritation. The 10MP camera punchout on the main display continues to be a bit of an eyesore, and those hoping for an under-display camera will be disappointed. It is the one element of the inner display that has not yet been resolved to a satisfying conclusion. Other than this, both the screens offer 3000 nits of peak brightness level and the antireflective coating makes the displays highly legible under direct sunlight and also under artificial lighting.Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 is powered by an octa-core Qualcomm Snapdragon Elite 8 Gen 5 chipset. The foldable smartphone comes in three variants – 16GB+1TB, 12GB+512GB and 12GB+512GB. In day-to-day use, the performance is exactly what you would expect from Qualcomm's current flagship silicon — instantaneous, effortless, and never the thing you are thinking about. App switching, multitasking across the larger inner canvas, gaming at high settings, and running Galaxy AI features simultaneously all produce no friction whatsoever.The main display of the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 creates a genuinely better multitasking environment than any previous Fold and also the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 handles the demands of running multiple applications side by side without any visible strain. For users who approach the Fold as a productivity device, the combination of this chip and the 4:3 inner display is more compelling than any previous Fold generation. The latest foldable from Samsung also handles games effortlessly, but the wider 4:3 inner display adds a dimension that raw processing power alone cannot. Games that support widescreen or tablet layouts benefit visibly from the additional horizontal real estate, with UI elements and game environments spreading across the canvas in a way that feels more immersive than the same title running on a conventional phone screen. Titles like BGMI and Asphalt run at their highest graphical settings without frame drops or thermal throttling becoming an issue during extended sessions, and the vapour chamber cooling keeps the device comfortable to hold throughout.The stereo speakers on the Galaxy Z Fold 8 are a genuine upgrade over previous generations and benefit directly from the wider chassis, which creates more physical separation between the speaker grilles than the taller, narrower Fold bodies allowed. In landscape orientation for gaming and video content, the stereo separation is wide enough to produce a convincing soundstage that holds up well for a phone. Dialogue in films is clear and well-defined, and music playback has enough body and volume to fill a small room without distortion at higher levels.Coming to software, the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 ships with Android 17 and One UI 9, and Samsung's software work specifically for the wider form factor is evident throughout. The taskbar adapts to the wider canvas intelligently, app layouts respond to the 4:3 and 3:4 orientations with purpose rather than simply stretching existing designs, and app continuity between cover and inner displays has become the kind of seamless experience that previously required patience and adjustment.Samsung continues to lead Android manufacturers in long-term software support, with seven major Android OS upgrades promised on the Z Fold 8. Buying a foldable at this price point and knowing it will receive updates through 2033 is a meaningful part of the value calculation, and it remains one of Samsung's clearest competitive advantages in the Android ecosystem. The deeper Gemini integration through Samsung's partnership with Google means AI assistance is available with genuine contextual awareness across native apps, and the large inner display creates space for AI-assisted workflows that simply could not exist on a smaller screen.Galaxy AI features are woven throughout One UI 9, and the wider 4:3 inner display makes them more practically useful than they were on previous Fold generations. The additional horizontal space allows AI assistance and active work to coexist in split-screen configurations that feel natural rather than cramped.Note Assist, Transcript Assist, and the Interpreter mode all benefit from the larger canvas, and the AI writing and summarisation tools feel genuinely integrated into the workflow rather than bolted on. My FanCam, which automatically crops and reframes video for social media, works well with the wider inner display proportions and is the kind of feature that the Fold's content creator audience will actually use.The agentic Galaxy AI capabilities which enable the assistant to take multi-step actions across the apps are more compelling on the Fold's larger screen than on any conventional phone, and the combination of One UI 9 and the 4:3 display creates a productivity environment that starts to make a credible argument for the foldable as a laptop complement rather than just a phone with a bigger screen.The Galaxy Z Fold 8 features a dual rear camera setup consisting of a 50MP primary camera with an f/1.8 aperture and a 50MP ultrawide camera with an F1.9 aperture, along with a 10MP front-facing camera on both the cover and inner displays.The 50MP ultrawide is the most meaningful camera upgrade over previous Fold generations, addressing the 12MP ultrawide that was consistently criticised as the system's weakest component. The consistency between primary and ultrawide output has improved substantially as a result, and the gap between the two lenses in real-world shooting is considerably narrower than it was on the Z Fold 7.The Z Fold 8 sports two outer cameras — a 50MP main and a 50MP ultrawide — while the Z Fold 8 Ultra features a 200MP main camera and a 10MP telephoto lens. The absence of a telephoto lens is the Z Fold 8's most significant camera compromise relative to the Ultra, and for buyers who use zoom regularly it is a genuine trade-off to factor into the choice between the two models. For those who do not, the dual 50MP system covers the vast majority of everyday shooting scenarios with competence and consistency.In daylight the primary sensor delivers detailed, accurately coloured images that hold up to scrutiny. Low-light performance is solid without being exceptional, and the Galaxy AI editing tools available on the inner display create a post-processing environment that is more comfortable to use than any conventional phone screen.Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 will surely impress you with its battery performance. The foldable Samsung smartphone houses a 4,800 mAh battery which comes with 45W wired fast charging support which is a meaningful step up from the 4,400mAh cell and 25W charging of the Z Fold 6, and the practical benefit is felt. Full-day endurance under heavy use, including significant time on the inner display, is reliably achievable. The 45W wired charging returns the battery to a usable level quickly enough that a lunchtime top-up genuinely covers an evening of heavier use. Wireless charging is supported, and the overall battery package feels appropriately sized for what the Z Fold 8 asks of it. It is not the area where the device tries to make its argument, but it no longer needs to be managed carefully to get through a day, which is the right place for it to be.The Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 is the most genuinely interesting design decision Samsung has made in the foldable space in seven years. The wider, passport-style form factor is not a minor iteration. It changes the fundamental logic of how a folded phone fits into daily life, makes the cover display genuinely usable for one-handed tasks, and creates an inner display experience for content consumption and multitasking that previous tall narrow Fold panels could not match. Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 comes with a starting price tag of Rs 1,79,999 and is an ideal choice for buyers who want to enter the Fold ecosystem for the first time, the Z Fold 8's new shape makes a more convincing case for why this form factor exists than any previous generation. That is perhaps the strongest endorsement it can receive.
Article Summary: The galaxy z fold 8 is samsung’s first wide-screen foldable smartphone which is light in weight and is identical to the shape of a passport. The front display measures 5.5-inch, which seems small, but its wide 10:16 aspect ratio makes it easy on the eyes.

Article Title: Nividia's 'Chinese trouble' continue, loses world's most-valuable company position to Apple
Article Text:
Apple’s strategy pays off

Apple has overtaken Nvidia as the world’s most valuable company, ending the chipmaker’s reign at the top go global markets. At Monday (July 27) close, Apple’s market capitalisation stood at $4.95 trillion, compared with Nvidia’s $4.77 trillion. The iPhone maker’s shares rose 1% ahead of its earnings report later this week, while Nvidia fell 5% amid investor concerns over the soaring costs of AI infrastructure. Nvidia had held the crown since June 2025, briefly touching a $5 trillion valuation last October. But in 2026, its shares have gained only 4%, compared with Apple’s 24% surge. Analysts say Nvidia’s “Chinese trouble” — including export restrictions and intensifying competition from Chinese AI startups — has added to investor unease, even as the company enters its third year of massive AI-driven sales growth.Apple has outperformed by avoiding heavy capital expenditures on AI, preferring to rent computing capacity rather than build its own. Investors have rewarded this cautious approach, especially as Nvidia’s costly megaprojects raise questions about sustainability. Apple is expected to reveal on Thursday how the global memory chip shortage has affected its finances, after the company raised Mac and iPad prices in June.While Nvidia remains central to the AI boom, investors are increasingly turning to memory chipmakers such as Micron Technology, SK Hynix, and Sandisk, which benefit from surging demand for data center infrastructure. The shift underscores how the AI race is broadening beyond GPUs to other critical components.Apple's recent rally has also been supported by long-awaited government approval to launch Apple Intelligence in China, a move that is expected to strengthen the company's growth prospects.Nvidia's shares came under pressure after reports that a new AI model developed by Chinese startup Moonshot rivals leading models from OpenAI and Anthropic, both of which rely on Nvidia's chips. The development has raised fresh concerns among investors that the massive spending on AI infrastructure could be nearing its peak.Adding to Apple's momentum, HSBC upgraded the stock to "buy" from "hold", citing the company's improving outlook.Apple "is now at an operational turning point," analyst Nicolas Cote-Colisson wrote. "Not only can the company stay away from the (too) high capex debate," but "it is also well placed to leverage its 2.5bn installed device base with its forthcoming revamped Apple Intelligence."
Article Summary: Apple overtakes chipmaker nvidia as world's most valuable company. Apple's market capitalisation now stands at $4.95 trillion, compared with nvidia's $ 4.77 trillion. Apple outperformed by avoiding heavy capital expenditures on ai, preferring to rent computing capacity rather than build its own.

Article Title: Netflix unveils ‘VOID’, an AI model that can change a movie plot
Article Text:
Netflix

How Netflix VOID works







Netflix has unveiled an AI model that can alter the scene. While this is nothing new, Netflix’s model not just remove objects from video, it understands what should happen next, essentially altering the causality. Most object-removal technology leaves a gap where something used to be and/ or fills it with a plausible-looking background. VOID goes a step further: after erasing an object from a scene, it calculates how the surrounding environment should realistically respond to its absence, and in the process it adjusts the behaviour of other elements in the frame accordingly.The model, called VOID, is a vision-language system designed to edit video footage with a level of contextual awareness that sets it apart from several existing tools.For example, imagine this scenario: A movie director has just wrapped up a multi-million dollar action sequence where the star drives straight into a fiery, head-on collision. The cars explode, debris scatters, and the scene is a wrap.But suddenly, there is request to change the scene: The character survives and drive off into the sunset instead. This would mean costly reshoots or millions spent on computer-generated graphics.Netflix’s VOID can alter the scene and digitally erase the collision, the second vehicle, the smoke, and the flying debris. It will then generate new, realistic footage of pristine pavement, making it look as though the main character simply drove down an empty, peaceful road.The AI’s ‘magic’ lies in its grasp of real-world physics. Let us understand this by a different example. If a video shows a person jumping into a pool and splashing water onto the deck, VOID can completely erase the person. It will then intelligently alter the water and the wet concrete, leaving behind a perfectly still, undisturbed pool as if nobody had ever jumped in.“To train the model, we generate a new paired dataset of counterfactual object removals using Kubric and HUMOTO, where removing an object requires altering downstream physical interactions. During inference, a vision-language model identifies regions of the scene affected by the removed object. These regions are then used to guide a video diffusion model that generates physically consistent counterfactual outcomes,” Netflix said.“Experiments on both synthetic and real data show that our approach better preserves consistent scene dynamics after object removal compared to prior video object removal methods,” the company added.Netflix isn’t keeping this powerful tool locked behind studio doors, and made the VOID model available to the public on the AI platform Hugging Face, allowing anyone to download and use it.While there are already several video-altering tools on the market, such as Runway, DiffuEraser, and ProPainter, the Netflix team claims VOID is vastly superior, as per The Register.
Article Summary: Netflix has unveiled an ai model that can alter the scene. While this is nothing new, netflix’s model not just remove objects from video, it understands what should happen next. Most object-removal technology leaves a gap where something used to be and/ or fills it with a plausible-looking background.

Article Title: AI data centers are causing 'stress' not just to tech companies, but also private insurers
Article Text:
Massive investments, growing risks



Unique challenges for data centre insurance companies





AI data centers are reportedly putting new pressure on the insurance industry. According to a CNBC report, experts warn that the rapid growth of these projects is becoming a “stress test” not just for tech companies, but also for private insurers and lenders. Consulting firm McKinsey estimates that global spending on data centers could reach $7 trillion by 2030. As costs rise, tech giants are increasingly relying on private equity, private credit and debt to fund these projects. The scale of investments is creating challenges for insurers.“When you put $10 to $20 billion plus in a single location, it creates capacity issues in the marketplace,” said Tom Harper, data center leader at insurance broker Gallagher as quoted in the CNBC report.He added that the sector has been a “real stress test” over the last few years, as insurers struggle to provide coverage for such large and complex projects. While these facilities are seen as high-quality assets, Harper said insuring them has become difficult due to their size and risk concentration.Private data center deals have crossed $10 billion regularly, with some reaching as high as $40 billion. Companies including Nvidia, Microsoft and BlackRock have already taken part in large investment deals.Rajat Rana, partner at Quinn Emanuel Urquhart & Sullivan, described the scale as unprecedented. “We’re talking about trillions of dollars, and almost going back to the same cycle where there’s almost no transparency about the financing structures — the scale is astronomical,” he said. He added that the boom in AI data centers could be “the largest peacetime investment project in human history.”Experts say the way these projects are financed is adding another layer of risk. Much of the funding is happening through complex and less transparent debt structures. Rana warned that this trend feels like “deja vu,” referring to past financial cycles. He said the lack of transparency could create risks for investors, insurers and pension funds.As stated in the CNBC report, data centers offer unique challenges due to their mix of real estate and advanced technology. Insurers are now designing custom policies to manage these risks. However, challenges remain. Large facilities are often located in areas prone to extreme weather, and they store expensive equipment, sometimes even before installation.Another key concern is the mismatch between the lifespan of data centers and the hardware they use. While data centers can last decades, GPUs — the chips powering AI — typically last around seven years. Rana described this as a “GPU debt treadmill,” saying, “This is almost like a treadmill that these AI data centers are running on.”He explained that companies may need to keep raising debt to upgrade infrastructure as technology evolves.
Article Summary: Private data center deals have crossed $10 billion regularly, with some reaching as high as $40 billion. Mckinsey estimates that global spending on data centers could reach $7 trillion by 2030. Tech giants are increasingly relying on private equity, private credit and debt to fund these projects.
